_comment: safety batch D English body (2026-11-06). OpenAI Evals open-source framework. Facts only from the official README, docs/run-evals.md and LICENSE.md captured on 2026-11-06; anything else is recorded as unknown.

axes.model_access: Your own model access is required: the README states that running evals needs an `OPENAI_API_KEY` and warns about API costs. docs/run-evals.md: by default any model on the OpenAI API is supported, any implementation of the `CompletionFn` protocol can be run by `oaieval`, and ready completion functions live in `evals/registry/completion_fns`. First-class support for other hosted providers: not stated officially.
axes.runtime: A local Python process; the README states "Minimum Required Version: Python 3.9". `pip install evals` to run evals, clone + `pip install -e .` to author them. The entry points are the terminal commands `oaieval` (single eval) and `oaievalset` (eval set), so it scripts into CI. The README's first line points hosted usage to the OpenAI Dashboard Evals docs; that cloud line was not captured in this pass.
axes.local_files: Eval definitions are YAML in the repo (`evals/registry/evals`, `evals/registry/eval_sets`) with implementations under `evals/elsuite`; dataset files come through Git-LFS into `evals/registry/data`. Logs default to local JSONL in `tmp/evallogs`, overridable with `--record_path`. Per the FAQ, a template-based or model-graded eval needs JSON data plus YAML and no evaluation code.
axes.background: A local long run, not a hosted queue. The official docs state `oaievalset` records finished evals in `/tmp/oaievalset/{model}.{eval_set}.progress.txt`, so a rerun picks up where it stopped; a single eval cannot be resumed mid-way and must restart. Concurrency is `EVALS_THREADS` / `EVALS_THREAD_TIMEOUT` (default 10 threads, 40-second timeout). What happens after the machine shuts down: not stated officially.
axes.tools: Extension points are the `CompletionFn` protocol, eval templates and model-graded YAML; the README routes prompt chains and tool-using agents to the Completion Function Protocol. Contribution is restricted: the README says evals with custom code are not accepted at present, while model-graded YAML files still are. MCP support, guardrails or interception mechanisms: not stated officially.
axes.context: There is no cross-session memory layer: one run is one round, and the artifacts are the local JSONL log plus the end-of-run report. Multi-turn or long-text workloads go through the eval templates in the repo (the FAQ shows the same dataset scored under different templates). Window truncation rules and default sample limits: no official text captured in this pass.
axes.permissions: The code is MIT; you run with your own API key, and the README describes private evals for testing your common LLM patterns without exposing the data publicly. The contribution terms need reading literally: contributed eval logic and data fall under the same MIT license, and "OpenAI reserves the right to use this data in future service improvements", with contributions subject to the platform Usage Policies. Server-side retention and training use: not stated officially.
axes.fit: Fits: running public benchmarks plus your own YAML evals in batch on your machine or in CI, reading logs as files rather than a console, and implementing CompletionFn for your own systems. Not a fit: wanting only a hosted console and hosted data plane (that is the Dashboard line), depending heavily on non-OpenAI models without writing an adapter, or needing sandboxing and tool approval as runtime boundaries.

sections.变更记录说明: The upstream repository is not flagged as archived on GitHub, but repository metadata shows the last push on 2026-04-14 (GitHub API verified 2026-11-06), more than 90 days before the verification date, so `lifecycle` is recorded as maintenance and the slower cadence is flagged here. This object has no standalone changelog page; changes are tracked through commit history, which was not reviewed item by item in this pass. The hosted Evals line referenced by the README's first line was not captured either - no official text obtained for it on the day.
sections.第一次怎么用:
1. First decide which line you want: the open-source framework described here, or hosted Evals in the Dashboard (the README's first line points to the latter).
2. Set `OPENAI_API_KEY` (required by the README to run evals) and note the official warning that API use is billed.
3. To run existing evals only: `pip install evals`; registry data lives in Git-LFS, fetched with the `git lfs fetch` / `git lfs pull` steps in the README.
4. In the terminal run `oaieval <model or completion function> <eval name>`; eval names come from the YAML under `evals/registry/evals`, batches via `oaievalset`.
5. Read the local JSONL logs under `tmp/evallogs` before considering Snowflake logging.
6. To attach your own system, implement a CompletionFn - but do not submit custom-code evals as contributions, which the README says are not accepted.

runs:
**This site has not completed end-to-end measured runs.** Nothing was executed with `oaieval` / `oaievalset`, no benchmark scores, accuracies or rankings are produced, and the registry contents were not audited.

This section only organizes statements that appear in the official README and docs/run-evals.md (installation, the two CLIs, log paths, concurrency and resume behaviour, contribution limits); each is tied to the sources list and the verification date.

**Suggested measurements** (all pointing at things the official pages do not answer):

- Effort to run a non-OpenAI model through a self-written `CompletionFn`
- Actual behaviour of `oaievalset` resume after a killed process, and the "hangs at the end" issue the README acknowledges
- Whether contributed eval data can be kept private end to end
unknowns:
- First-class support for hosted providers other than OpenAI (official text covers the OpenAI API plus custom CompletionFn only)
- Dashboard-hosted Evals feature surface and data terms: no official text captured on the day
- Context-window truncation rules and the default per-eval sample limit
- Resume semantics after shutdown or network loss (official text only covers the `oaievalset` progress file)
- MCP integration, guardrail or interception mechanisms
- Server-side retention and training use of run data
- Commit-by-commit change review (not done in this pass)
